title: Exercise: counterexample-guided synthesis (2), more per round
description: Part 2 of the weighted voting exercise; it starts from the solution of part 1. Each round learns one coalition. Learn several per round (the readme guides you), then press Check exercise in the Instances tab.
readme:
# Counterexample-guided synthesis: more per round (part 2)

Do part 1 first: this starter is its worked solution, the basic CEGIS loop.

## Look first

Run `council6` and count the rounds: each one costs an optimal solve of A, and each one learns
a single coalition. A check can return more than one: there are usually many coalitions that
the candidate gets wrong.

## The task

Learn **several counterexamples per round**. Ask C for up to a few of them and expand A with each
one, then solve A again. You need:

- `XS = C.models(assume G(M), limit 3)`: a list of up to 3 models of C (empty if there is none).
- `XS.size`, and `for X in XS:`.
- One `A.expand(refine, cex = ...)` per counterexample (each gets its own `k`).

Another way: let the check pick several wrong coalitions in one model (`1 { bad(S) : coalition(S) } 3`
does not quite do it: why not?).

## Check yourself

**Check exercise**: every optimum, a sound audit on `dictator3`, at most 9 candidates on `council6`,
8 on `majority5` and 6 on `steps6`.

## Questions

1. What is the trade-off of a larger limit? Look at the time of A's solves in the Statistics tab.
2. Are the counterexamples of one round different from each other in a useful way? Would "the
   coalitions furthest from the quota" be better ones? (Guide chapter 6, "Asking for the best
   counterexample".)
3. With all counterexamples (no limit), how many rounds are left, and what has the loop become?

fragments.name: shared
fragments.text:
% The instance (Instances tab) gives the players, player(P) for P = 1..n, and the rule to
% imitate: wins(S) for every coalition S that wins. A coalition is a number 0..2^n - 1:
% player P is in coalition S when bit P - 1 of S is set. The constants n and wmax (the
% largest weight) come with the instance.
coalition(0..2**n-1).
in(P,S) :- player(P), coalition(S), (S / 2**(P-1)) \ 2 = 1.
fragments.description: Added to every solver: coalitions and their members.

fragments.name: abstraction
fragments.text:
% Solver A: a weight 0..wmax for every player and a quota; the lightest first.
1 { w(P,0..wmax) } 1 :- player(P).
1 { quota(1..n*wmax) } 1.
#minimize { W,P : w(P,W) }.
#show w/2.
#show quota/1.

% One coalition that an earlier candidate got wrong: from now on, every candidate must get it
% right. A copy of the specification for one input (cex(k, bad(S)) comes from the loop).
#program refine(k).
weight(k,X) :- cex(k,bad(S)), X = #sum { W,P : in(P,S), w(P,W) }.
:- cex(k,bad(S)), wins(S), weight(k,X), quota(Q), X < Q.
:- cex(k,bad(S)), not wins(S), weight(k,X), quota(Q), X >= Q.
fragments.description: Solver A: a weight for every player and a quota.

fragments.name: glue
fragments.description: The interface atoms: every glue(T) makes T an interface atom.

fragments.name: check
fragments.text:
% Solver C looks for a counterexample: one coalition that the weights classify wrongly.
1 { bad(S) : coalition(S) } 1.
weight(S,X) :- bad(S), X = #sum { W,P : in(P,S), w(P,W) }.
:- bad(S), wins(S), weight(S,X), quota(Q), X >= Q.
:- bad(S), not wins(S), weight(S,X), quota(Q), X < Q.
#show bad/1.
fragments.description: Solver C: a coalition that the weights classify wrongly.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction
solver C = shared + check
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Counterexample-guided synthesis: the lightest weights that classify every coalition seen so far
# correctly. If no coalition is classified wrongly, they are optimal; otherwise learn that
# coalition (a copy of the specification for it) and ask again.
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if not X:
        accept M
        stop
    A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(bad/1))

instances.facts:
% Player 1 decides alone.
player(1..3).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(1,S).

% Everyone must agree.
player(1..3).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), #count { P : in(P,S) } = 3.

% Simple majority of five.
player(1..5).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), #count { P : in(P,S) } >= 3.

% the chair (1) and at least two others, or all three others
player(1..4).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(1,S), #count { P : in(P,S), P > 1 } >= 2.
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(2,S), in(3,S), in(4,S).

% players 1 and 2 have a veto; they need at least two of 3, 4, 5
player(1..5).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(1,S), in(2,S), #count { P : in(P,S), P > 2 } >= 2.

% (1 and 2) or (3 and 4): not a weighted game
player(1..4).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(1,S), in(2,S).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(3,S), in(4,S).

% 1 alone with any two others, or 2 and 3 with any two of 4, 5, 6, or everyone but 1
player(1..6).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(1,S), #count { P : in(P,S), P > 1 } >= 2.
wins(S) :- coalition(S), in(2,S), in(3,S), #count { P : in(P,S), P > 3 } >= 2.
wins(S) :- coalition(S), #count { P : in(P,S), P > 1 } >= 5.

% 1 counts thrice, 2 and 3 twice, the rest once; quota 6
player(1..6).
wins(S) :- coalition(S), #sum { 3,P : in(P,S), P = 1; 2,P : in(P,S), P = 2..3; 1,P : in(P,S), P > 3 } >= 6.

exercise.text: Learn several counterexamples per round. Every instance must still give its optimum (two-pairs: no solution), the audit must be sound on dictator3, council6 must need at most 9 candidates, majority5 at most 8 and steps6 at most 6.
